deck: 30 Thinking in Java::17 Containers in Depth

cards.front: Why does the containers library contain classes named AbstractSet, AbstractList…?
cards.back: They are skeletons that implement most of an interface, so your own container only fills the gaps
cards.extra: The book's advice: you almost never need them. They are scaffolding for people writing a new collection type, not part of normal use.

cards.front: Which two methods must agree for a hashed container to work?
cards.back: equals() and hashCode() — equal objects must return the same hash
cards.extra: HashSet/HashMap find a bucket by hash, then confirm identity by equals. Break the contract and a stored object becomes unfindable even though it is still inside.

cards.front: What breaks if you override equals but not hashCode?
cards.back: Lookups fail: the object lands in one bucket but is searched for in another
cards.extra: Two equal objects then hash differently, so map.get misses. This is why IDEs generate both together, always.

cards.front: What does LinkedHashMap preserve that HashMap does not?
cards.back: Insertion order (or access order, if you configure it that way)
cards.extra: HashMap gives no ordering guarantee at all. LinkedHashMap costs a little memory for the links and is the usual choice when iteration order matters.

cards.back: Keys iterate in sorted order, by natural ordering or a Comparator
cards.extra: TreeMap is the implementation. Sorting costs O(log n) per operation instead of the O(1) average of hashing.

cards.back: Replaces every element of a List with the same object reference
cards.extra: It does not copy. Five slots pointing at one mutable object is rarely what you want — use a generator or a loop that creates new instances.
